item.title: JD Vance faces tough questions on Iran war, immigration and gas prices in town hall
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In an hour-long town hall hosted by CBS News, Vice President JD Vance argued the Trump administration's handling of the economy and Iran strategy will pay dividends in the future. He was also pressed on the Trump administration's controversial immigration tactics, widespread discontent about the cost of living and his own political future during "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance," which aired Saturday evening and was hosted by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil. Vance took questions from voters in Michigan, a swing state that helped propel Vance and President Trump to victory in 2024 — and is the host of a tight Senate race that could help determine which party wins control of the upper chamber in next month's midterm elections. Vance says he hasn't decided if he'll run for president If he decides to run for president in 2028, the vice president is widely viewed as an early frontrunner in the Republican primaries and a possible heir to Mr. Trump's political movement. Mr. Trump has called Vance his "most likely" GOP successor and has joked about a potential contest between Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Asked by Dokoupil if there's any chance he won't run, Vance said: "Of course there's a chance." "The way that I think about life, big life decisions — my wife will tell you this — is I'm a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it," said Vance, adding that he'll "have to think about it." He also noted that he and his wife, Usha Vance, have four young children, and the second lady "has never loved politics," though "she loves public service." On economy, Vance says "we're turning the ship around" but it will take time Several town hall attendees asked Vance about cost-of-living issues. The topic weighs heavily in the midterms, and has demonstrated it's a liability for Republicans based on CBS News polling. Voter dissatisfaction with inflation and the state of the economy under the Biden administration helped bring Mr. Trump and Vance to power, but polls indicate that most voters are still unhappy with the economy and hold the Trump administration responsible. Sandy Johnson said the family entertainment center she owns is "barely making ends meet," and asked when she can expect changes "so that the normal American has money to spend on small businesses." The vice president argued it could take some time. "What broke the United States, as much as I might like to criticize Joe Biden, but it was a bipartisan, multi-generational failure to under-invest in American workers, to under-invest in American manufacturing, to ship all of our good jobs overseas," Vance said. "If all the good jobs are overseas, then people here in Michigan can't spend money at your family business." He pointed to promises of new foreign investment in the United States, and growth plans by the three major Detroit-area automakers, General Motors, Ford and Chrysler parent Stellantis. "We are turning the tide on this," Vance said, referring to the decline in U.S. manufacturing. "And I think there are all these things I pointed to that show signs of progress. But Sandy, I'll be the first person to tell you that, just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around." Since Mr. Trump returned to office last year, the unemployment rate has remained low, but inflation has remained stubbornly higher than the Federal Reserve's 2%-per-year target, eating into Americans' wages. The number of manufacturing jobs has also remained roughly flat. Asked by Dokoupil about Mr. Trump's assessment of an "A+" economy , Vance said the president was referring to new investments, "but he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first before you can employ the workers working in those factories." Vance later said: "I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around." Iran and energy: "I recognize that gas prices are too high right now" One of the biggest pressure points on Americans' wallets is the Iran war , which has kept oil prices high even as the U.S. and Iran have refrained from active fighting in recent weeks. Keshon Wheatley, a barber from Detroit, told Vance that he voted for Mr. Trump in 2020 and 2024, in large part because he gave the president credit for low gas prices during his first term. Now, gas prices are far higher — and he said he plans to vote for Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , not Republican Mike Rogers. Vance pointed to Iran's attacks on oil tankers. "We've never had a situation like this, where you have effectively the largest state sponsor of terrorism that's trying to completely choke off world energy supply," the vice president said, arguing that "if we just … left, and we let the Iranians control shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, what that would mean is you would pay a lot more for gasoline." Asked how long it will take for prices to ease, Vance said, "When this conflict is over, we are going to see gas prices come down." He said oil is still being exported from the Middle East because of efforts by the U.S. military to allow ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. On the competitive Michigan Senate race, he argued El-Sayed — a frequent critic of the Iran war — has not offered a solution to the problem, and gave Rogers credit for calling for the war to end. "He's been remarkably independent about this," Vance said of Rogers. Dokoupil asked Vance why the U.S. hasn't decisively won the Iran war, which has dragged on for longer than Mr. Trump initially expected. Vance argued that "in some ways we have won decisively," but "the enemy gets a vote here." The vice president — who participated in negotiations with Iran over the summer — defended the president's Iran strategy, and said the Trump administration is looking for a "final firm commitment from the Iranians that they're not going to rebuild their nuclear program." Man whose wife died in Iranian strike decries "fundamental failures" The Iran war has also imposed human costs, with 21 U.S. service members killed and hundreds injured since the conflict began in late February. In the war's early hours, six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed in an Iranian strike on a site in Kuwait, including Master Sgt. Nicole Amor . Her husband, Joey Amor, asked Vance about reports that the facility in Kuwait was not adequately secured. "Though the Iranian drone was the weapon that killed my wife, there were a lot of mistakes and a lot of fundamental failures that led up to that," Amor said, asking Vance "how this administration is gonna start holding those leaders accountable." Vance said he didn't doubt there were failures , but "sometimes information doesn't filter up to me." He vowed to "take every single failure extremely seriously." He also noted that cheap drones have changed warfare, and "we have changed a lot of our tactics to try to suppress that drone fire, to try to protect our troops to make it so that more people don't have to pay the ultimate sacrifice." Vance also said: "I know that there are some issues with, for example … where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake and that we could do better on. And we have changed that." Nun presses Vance on immigration tactics Sister Nancy Sylvester, a member of the Sister Servants of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, asked Vance about the Trump administration's approach to immigration enforcement . She asked Vance, a fellow Catholic, "how you would justify [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactics] to people of faith," and "what policies would you advocate to try to promote more compassionate and [respectful] behavior toward our immigrant sisters and brothers." Vance responded, "We're trying to strike a balance between: How do we do law enforcement, but how do we also do it humanely, and how do we not do so little law enforcement that you actually empower some of the worst people in the world." Vance later said most ICE agents are "amazing people who are patriots," but some of them "make mistakes" or "really screw up." He added that "obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up." Asked if any major mistakes by ICE come to mind, Vance responded that "there are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE." Another town hall attendee pressed Vance on some of the administration's rhetoric around immigration, including Vance's own comments that likened some holders of employment-based H-1B visas to "foreign indentured servants." Vance responded, "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me." He said his comments were "not a criticism of the H-1B holder." "That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker, bring somebody else in, and knows that person, if they complain, if they get too uppity at work, if they have a disagreement with their boss, they couldn't just lose their job, … they can be shipped back to their country of origin," Vance said. "And I think that gives employers way too much power." He said, "My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant." But he said he is seeking "to make it so that we can have a country with some baseline of social cohesion and sense of community, because what happens when too many people come to the United States, even if they're very good people, … [is] it changes the country in very profound ways." "D.C. is a corrupt town," but Vance says no evidence Trump is participating in it Dokoupil asked Vance about polling that indicates many voters are concerned about corruption and believe Mr. Trump is prioritizing his own personal business interests while in office. Vance said , "I've never seen anything like that from the president." "Yes, D.C. is a corrupt town," Vance said, but "I have not seen a single shred of evidence that he participates or sanctions in that corruption." Dokoupil also asked about a string of recent reports, including Mr. Trump's cryptocurrency earnings and U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's ouster over allegations that she asked a person seeking help from the Trump administration to wire her $100,000. Guilfoyle has denied all wrongdoing. Mr. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest. Vance responded : "If somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences." The vice president also said he will "follow the law" if a Democratic Congress launches investigations and subpoenas the Trump administration. Data centers need to be "good community citizens" A major point of tension in many communities across the country is the explosion in data center development , as the artificial intelligence boom leads to insatiable demand for computing power. Mr. Trump has enthusiastically backed the AI industry, casting it as an engine of economic growth and a key area of competition with China. He has also argued data center construction can be beneficial to local communities, bringing jobs and investments in crucial technology. But many voters have raised concerns about noise, disruption and pressure on the electrical grid, leading to calls for development to slow down. Vance took a question from one Michigan resident who lives across the street from a data center and said the constant buzzing has made "opening our windows to let in a breeze … a luxury that we could no longer enjoy." The vice president said "data centers can be good" and can also "cause real problems." He said his view is that data centers should be "good community citizens," offering more tax revenue to local governments. The data centers should also not lead to higher residential utility bills, Vance said. "Some of the economic benefits they're generating, they can't just go to a few tech billionaires," he said. "It has to go to the community writ large." Watch the full episode of "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" streaming on Paramount+ , YouTube , CBS News 24/7 and CBSNews.com . This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jd-vance-cbs-town-hall-highlights-michigan/

item.title: What are self-replicating 'AI worms', and why is Anthropic worried about them?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
‘Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.’ Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/Reuters Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about. Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each. Related: AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devices In addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort. “It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.” The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet. That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the Russian NotPetya and North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide. Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. The Anthropic team predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities. What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.” Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House. “The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.” Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows a paper published by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm. “The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan. Guan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said. “Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne. “It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own.” Anthropic did not respond to an interview request. Outside Washington, many in the AI and security worlds believe greater government oversight of AI is now essential. But members of Congress have introduced mutually conflicting bills, while the White House has so far created only a small review board . Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants. “The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.” This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://tech.yahoo.com/cybersecurity/articles/self-replicating-ai-worms-why-133000706.html

item.title: Trump approval hits record low, handing Democrats a clear midterm edge
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Two weeks from Election Day, Republicans face a bleak political landscape. President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to a new low, and support for Democrats in the race for control of Congress is rising as inflationary pressures contribute to an acrid mood among voters, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll. Trump's approval among U.S. adults now stands at 33 percent, with 66 percent disapproving; 52 percent said they disapprove strongly. That approval rating is four percentage points lower than in July and eight points lower than at this point last year. It's lower than at any point in his first term. Among likely voters, Trump's approval is 38 percent, with 62 percent disapproving. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The poll also finds that, for the first time in more than a decade, Democrats are seen as more trusted to deal with the economy. In the competition for control of the House, Democrats hold an eight-point lead among registered and likely voters, an improvement for the party since The Post's July poll, when the Democratic lead was three points with registered voters. Trump is central to Republicans' struggles. In a separate question, the poll asked voters whether they would rather have a Democratic-led Congress acting as a check on Trump or a Republican one to support his agenda. By 58 percent to 39 percent, registered voters said they prefer the Democrats. That margin is roughly double what it was a year ago. The collective results of the new survey reveal an electorate that has lost faith in the president, is deeply worried about his decision to go to war with Iran, is feeling the effects of that war - especially the price of gasoline - on their pocketbooks and now has more confidence in Democrats than Republicans to deal with major issues. Today, 72 percent say the country is heading in the wrong direction, up five points since April. The new survey findings do not predict how individual House or Senate races will turn out in November. But they help to explain why Republicans are on the defensive in these final weeks, even in areas where they have traditionally held a strong advantage. Republicans still enjoy an overall lead in money to pour into political advertising that they hope will hold back the Democratic tide. Tellingly, those resources are shifting to protect some candidates in redder areas, a sign of the growing concerns among party leaders and strategists about the overall climate. As always, the question of who turns out to vote will decide how individual races go, with many of the most competitive Senate races still in the balance. Nationally, Democrats have a big advantage among those who said they're "certain to vote" or have already done so, but Republicans fare relatively well among voters who turned out in the 2024 or 2022 elections, which are also strong predictors of voting. One critical unknown is how many of Trump's 77 million voters from the 2024 election will cast ballots. Midterm turnout is always lower than in presidential years and Republicans have had a harder time turning out their supporters when Trump is not on the ballot. The poll echoes those challenges. Democratic registered voters are more likely than Republicans to say they are certain to vote or have already done so, 75 percent versus 67 percent. While 75 percent of Republicans who support the MAGA movement say they're certain to vote, that drops to 57 percent among non-MAGA Republicans (though more than a quarter of these non-MAGA Republicans said they prefer Democrats in control of the next Congress). By contrast, 79 percent of Democrats who support the Democratic Socialists of America say they are certain to vote, as do 73 percent of nonsocialist Democrats. Presidential approval has long been one of the most important indicators of how a midterm election will go. Based on history, Republicans are poised to lose seats from their narrow House majority and likely to lose control of the chamber next month. But how many is more difficult to predict because, in contrast to some past years, there are fewer swing districts. Republicans may also retain backing from voters who expressed only limited dissatisfaction with the president. The Post-ABC-Ipsos poll finds that among the 10 percent of likely voters who said they "somewhat disapprove" of Trump's performance, 58 percent prefer the Republican candidate for the House. Economic issues stand as a major threat to the GOP's hold on the House and Senate. Trump's economic approval rating has fallen to 28 percent, down from 33 percent in July, 41 percent in February and 49 percent at this point in the 2018 midterm election campaign. About 3 in 4 Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation and the cost of living in the United States. By a 3-1 margin, Americans said the state of the economy is either not so good or poor. Most Republicans (53 percent) rate the economy positively compared with 9 percent of Democrats and 16 percent of independents. At this point in 2022, when President Joe Biden was in office, impressions of the economy were almost identically negative. But in a sign of how party allegiance can affect attitudes, 54 percent of Democrats then rated the economy positively, compared with 8 percent of Republicans and 16 percent of independents. Economic strains on many Americans are great enough that 48 percent say they are financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025. That represents the highest percentage saying this about any president in Post-ABC polls since 1986. Among these financially stressed Americans, 78 percent favor Democrats for Congress, along with 71 percent of independents. Affordability is an issue that nearly all candidates are talking about this fall and the survey points to many areas of difficulty for families. The biggest is the cost of gasoline. In February, before Trump launched the war with Iran, 71 percent said gasoline was affordable. Today, as the war has disrupted supplies and shipping, pushing up gasoline and diesel prices significantly, perceptions have flipped, with 71 percent now saying gasoline is not affordable. Majorities also say groceries, health care and home energy are unaffordable, all up significantly since before the Iran war. Fewer than 4 in 10 said going out to dinner is affordable, down from half who said this in February. The shift against the president ripples throughout the survey. On Iran, 65 percent said it was a mistake to take military action and 68 percent disapprove of the way Trump has dealt with U.S. allies. Roughly 6 in 10 disapprove of his handling of immigration, a sharp departure from the beginning of his second term when 50 percent said they approved. A majority (56 percent) said Trump has gone too far in deporting undocumented immigrants, which compares with 48 percent in April 2025 as the deportation effort was beginning. Trump's negative ratings are boosted by significant criticism from his 2024 voters, including 23 percent who disapprove of his overall performance, 31 percent who disapprove of his management of the economy and 38 percent who disapprove of his handling of inflation. Most of these critics said they support Republicans for Congress, but they're far less certain about casting ballots this year than Trump voters who approve of him. Trump is judged harshly on several measures of his commitment to fundamental principles of democracy. At least 6 in 10 people said he is not committed to protecting freedom of the press and freedom of speech, free and fair elections, and respecting the authority of Congress or the courts. Beyond major issues, the public disapproves of the ways Trump has conducted himself in office. The poll finds that 66 percent said he is using the presidency to enrich himself, up from 56 percent last fall. Eight in 10 think it is inappropriate that he has pushed to put his name on the Kennedy Center in Washington (59 percent view this as "completely inappropriate"), and 74 percent say it's inappropriate that the federal government paid for television ads promoting Trump and his policies. Overall, 66 percent said they see Trump as "too extreme." The dissatisfaction with Trump inevitably has spilled onto a Republican Party that has been remade in his image. Registered voters said they trust Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy by 40 percent to 33 percent, the first Democratic advantage on the economy in Post-ABC polling since 2014. Voters split about evenly on this question in April and July of this year. Democrats also hold double-digit advantages on trust to handle inflation and the cost of living. Democrats are seen as more trustworthy on many issues even though 54 percent of U.S. adults have an unfavorable view of the party, perhaps because even more Americans - 63 percent - dislike the Republican Party. The Republican Party is seen as too extreme by 55 percent of U.S. adults, compared with 36 percent who see the Democratic Party that way. Americans hold negative impressions of the president's MAGA movement and of democratic socialism, which has roiled the Democratic Party this year. But the MAGA movement is seen even more negatively at 69 percent unfavorable compared with 59 percent unfavorable toward democratic socialism. item.title: Trump's most controversial moves have something in common: This DOJ office
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When White House officials wanted to know if President Donald Trump could send the U.S. military to help capture President Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a special unit in the Justice Department assured them it was legal. When the administration was preparing to strike suspected drug traffickers’ boats on the open sea without congressional approval, the same small unit declared the action permissible. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. When the White House asked if the Presidential Records Act was constitutional, the office ruled it was not, giving Trump the apparent green light to save fewer records from his second term. As the Trump administration pushes the bounds of executive power, the Justice Department unit known as the Office of Legal Counsel, or OLC, has affirmed some of its most high-profile and controversial actions - even as many experts question their legitimacy and some are later struck down by the courts. Tucked away on the Justice Department’s fifth floor, the two dozen or so lawyers at the OLC are charged with assessing the legality of actions the executive branch wants to take, especially those that are novel or likely to be contentious. Much of its work, particularly on national security matters, remains shielded from public view, but some of the office’s conclusions have emerged in often dense legal opinions. The OLC during Trump’s second term is not the first to be accused of adopting shaky reasoning to justify a president’s policies. Under President Barack Obama, the OLC wrote a controversial rationale for launching a deadly drone attack on a U.S. citizen overseas. Under President George W. Bush, the office justified the used of “enhanced interrogation” - what some call torture - against enemy combatants, including waterboarding. But because Trump has advanced so many controversial policies - including imposing global tariffs, refusing to spend congressionally allocated funds and pushing to more broadly deploy the National Guard - the OLC now faces particular scrutiny. Critics contend that during Trump’s second term, the OLC is sometimes responding to legal questions that appear personal to Trump, rather than addressing live policy debates, as is typical. For instance, Trump had quibbled over the Presidential Records Act after he was indicted in Florida for allegedly mishandling classified materials. These critics said the OLC opinion on this act seemed aimed at Trump’s prior issues with the law, rather than any active policy issues. “It is not inconsistent with the type of advice OLC of any flavor, Democrats or Republicans, would give to other presidents,” said Carlos Uriarte, a Justice Department political appointee during the Biden administration who worked closely with the OLC. “What’s different is that this administration seems to be more willing to go into theoretical questions that are not before them.” Trump’s OLC is headed by T. Elliot Gaiser, a 37-year-old former solicitor general of Ohio described by current and former colleagues as a constitutional originalist who, like Trump, has an expansive view of executive power. Gaiser, who represented Trump’s losing presidential campaign in 2020 and refuses to acknowledge Joe Biden won that election, said his role in the Justice Department is to provide honest legal advice, not push for any particular outcome. “We’re the least interested in advocating, [and] the most interested in saying, ‘Here’s our frank view of where we think we stand in respect to the law,’” Gaiser told The Washington Post in a rare interview. His sparsely decorated office is filled with bound books of legal opinions, which surround a desk Gaiser proudly says is believed to have once been used by former Supreme Court justice Antonin Scalia, who headed the OLC under President Gerald Ford. People who know and have worked with Gaiser spoke positively about him, with former associates describing him as “brilliant.” Gaiser clerked on the Supreme Court for Samuel A. Alito Jr. when the justice wrote the landmark opinion restricting abortion access. As OLC head, Gaiser has written conservative opinions backing restrictions around abortion access, expanded gun access and greater White House authority. Gaiser said he has not hesitated to tell the White House when its ideas should not be enacted, though he declined to share specifics. Gaiser, and others familiar with the office, noted that the president is not required to listen to the OLC. Much of OLC advice is shared privately. As a result, public perceptions of the OLC are largely shaped by the opinions it releases, even as they represent only a portion of its work. The office’s role could become even more central if Democrats take control of Congress. The office recently approved an expanded view of executive privilege, for example, which Democrats fear will be used to shield Trump’s associates from testifying before Congress. Gaiser’s office could also get asked to provide legal advice if outcomes are challenged during and after next month’s midterms. The office has already determined that the executive branch can legally seek a state’s voter rolls and share them with immigration authorities - a key part of the Trump administration’s strategy to identify noncitizen voters as it tries to argue that voter fraud is rampant. Asked during the interview in his office who won the 2020 election, Gaiser demurred, citing his work as a lawyer for Trump’s campaign that year. He cannot say publicly who won, Gaiser said, because that would reveal too much about the privileged legal advice he gave Trump campaign officials when he was their attorney. “Joe Biden was sworn in as the president. He was certified the winner of the election by the Congress,” Gaiser said. “What I privately think happened in the 2020 election - what advice I provided to the president as the head of the campaign or to others in the campaign, the other campaign lawyers - that’s the kind of stuff I just really can’t get into .” Although many Trump appointees display sharp elbows and make frequent appearances on cable news shows, Gaiser takes a lower profile, even as his work is attracting increased attention, including from Democratic lawmakers and federal courts. After the OLC declared in April that the Presidential Records Act was unconstitutional, a federal court responded to lawsuits and said that, at least for now, the White House had to preserve records as normal. Advocacy groups are fighting to unseal the OLC’s memo justifying the deadly boat strikes in international waters. One former OLC attorney, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer a sensitive assessment, said the office’s opinions are based on shoddy legal arguments. Under previous administrations, “you have opinions that at least try to grapple with counterarguments,” but that is not the case today, the former OLC lawyer said. Gaiser sharply disputes the assertion that his office’s opinions are not high-quality, saying he and his lawyers deliver honest, accurate assessments. “There is a continuum with the advice you give. You can say, this is lawful but risky. This is lawfully safe. This is unlawful,” Gaiser said. “OLC has a measure of independent counsel that we offer.” During the first Trump administration, the OLC pushed back on some of the president’s most explosive actions. Steve Engel, then head of the OLC, testified about the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol that he had advised Trump appointees that some of their plans to question the results of the 2020 presidential election were not legal. Under Engel, the OLC also advised that an executive order ending birthright citizenship - the legal principal that virtually everyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen - would be unconstitutional, according to multiple people familiar with the matter, and the president did not issue one. But when Trump became president a second time, he issued an order to end birthright citizenship on his first day in office. The OLC did not review it or the other executive orders Trump issued immediately upon his return, according to two people familiar with the matter. The Supreme Court later affirmed birthright citizenship in a ruling that Trump called a “miscarriage of justice.” Gaiser, who was confirmed in July 2025, had not taken office at that point, and said his office has since reviewed all of the president’s executive orders before they are issued. The OLC attracted a burst of attention in August when it issued an opinion on executive privilege, which can shield communications between presidents and their aides. The office declared that the doctrine covers not only official advisers, but can also expand to cover outside associates consulted by the president in certain circumstances. The opinion was released as the American Bar Association was suing the Trump administration over its efforts to sanction law firms that hired Trump’s perceived foes or took on cases he disliked. The ABA is seeking testimony from Boris Epshteyn, one of Trump’s outside advisers. The ABA assailed the OLC opinion as self-serving and suspiciously timed. But Michael Edney, who worked at the OLC under Bush, said the opinion’s reading of executive privilege was not unreasonable, given the importance that some presidents place on outside consultation. “It’s not all that crazy to me,” he said. Most experts said that while OLC lawyers are not required to be blind to the president’s agenda, they cannot simply interpret the law to suit his priorities. Former OLC employees said the office should not be a rubber stamp, regardless of whether the president heeds its opinions. “In the executive branch, like everywhere else in the world, lawyers give advice and clients make decisions,” Edney said. “Their job is to provide legal advice.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/18/meet-small-doj-unit-approving-some-trumps-most-controversial-policies/

item.title: 'It's like a war zone': Fresh clashes break out in Paris after historic day of unrest
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Sybille de La Hamaide PARIS, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Fresh clashes broke out in Paris on Sunday a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with protests over high prices leaving one demonstrator dead, thousands arrested and shops across the country looted or damaged. Nationwide demonstrations ‌erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the ‌country. One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris. Police made more than 2,000 arrests across France, while more than 600 officers were injured, the interior minister said. "It's like a war zone here," said ​Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who had come to Paris with his children to visit a friend and said the protests forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, a trouble hotspot on Saturday. Police again clashed with protesters and fired tear gas at Place de la Republique on Sunday afternoon, and packs of bikes were set on fire. A Reuters witness estimated several hundred protesters were in the area. In Marseille, France's second largest city, the local prefecture also reported some incidents in the afternoon, with attempts made by groups to break into shops. More ‌than half a million people joined marches in scores of ⁠cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services. President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 8 p.m. local time (1800 GMT) on Sunday, his office said. Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at ⁠Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt. The government has blamed the violence on hard-left and ultra-left groups, as well as criminals who it said instigated the looting. French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen called for calm, saying France must not become accustomed to images of the country being battered, ​abused, ​and ransacked. "Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a form of expression. And chaos cannot serve ​as a project for France," she said in a video address. SEVERAL HUNDRED ‌SHOPS DAMAGED While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers. A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said several hundred shops had been damaged on Saturday. In Limoges, southwestern France, Mayor Guillaume Guerin denounced the chaos after the city's 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze and largely destroyed in an arson attack on Saturday, drawing comparisons to the 2019 fire that devastated Paris's Notre-Dame Cathedral. "There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, ‌and the people inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters. He threatened to resign if the ​city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall. PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION TO TAKE PLACE NEXT YEAR The ​unrest has increased pressure on President Macron and his government ahead of a ​presidential election due next year. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals. Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for ‌business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair ​the damage and be held accountable for their ​intention to sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement. Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted in his city, while Marseille Mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial aid to support those businesses impacted by the violence. French retailer Carrefour's CEO Alexandre Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops ​had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from ‌the damage running into the tens of millions of euros. The protests began last month over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into ​a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living. (Reporting by Sybille de La Hamaide; Additional reporting by Natasa Bansagi, Janis Laizans, ​Abdul Saboor, Clotaire Achi, Marc Leras; Editing by Richard Lough, Elaine Hardcastle and Jan Harvey) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/france-faces-aftermath-worst-unrest-094920368.html

item.title: U.S. taking Putin's side would be a 'historic mistake,' says Zelensky
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S. formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake,” but said he still sees President Donald Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill. “We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday, referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.” Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, saying in an executive order that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.” Passed with bipartisan support and signed by Trump last month , the sanctions were intended to target Russia’s revenue streams by punishing global buyers of Russian oil and gas. The waiver came days after a deal with Putin to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar. At the same time, Zelenskyy said, U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” blinding Ukraine to incoming ballistic missiles, while limits have been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercept jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe the decision to limit Starlink, imposed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, came in response to a “message from American government.” The U.S. has been Ukraine’s most significant backer across four and a half years of war, but personal relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have appeared severely strained in recent weeks, with each offering public criticisms of the other. Asked about Trump’s remark this week that the Ukrainian leader was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelenskyy said he was “very honest” with Trump. “Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.” Zelenskyy, who accused the U.S. of betraying Kyiv last week, said that his feelings have not changed. He warned that Trump’s diesel deal with Russia “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.” Announcing the deal week, Trump expressed hopes that it would go some way to address soaring fuel costs. But Zelenskyy said the deal wouldn’t have “a real influence” on the price of oil in the U.S. because the rising prices were due to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine. “I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said. Of the prospect of the U.S. more formally siding with Russia, he said: “If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand.” Zelenskyy said it was a “pity” Trump had waived the sanctions in a bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who he said was “a great supporter of peace and of Ukraine.” “He invested his life and time because he really believed in Ukraine,” he said. In a separate interview on “Meet the Press,” Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., defended Trump’s decision to lift the Russia sanctions. “He’s trying to walk this fine balance between trying to be able to put pressure on Russia, but also to be able to help the American people, so he is choosing the American people first is what he’s doing,” Lankford said, pointing to high gas prices. Asked whether Trump’s moves indicate the president is siding with Putin, Lankford said that Trump was “siding with the free people of Ukraine,” adding later that Trump was working to get the two countries “to the table to be able to negotiate.” The war has seen little recent movement on the frontline, with Russia continuing to occupy around a fifth of Ukraine. Trump had vowed to end the conflict within days of his second term, but peace talks have effectively stalled, with Ukraine saying that Russia has rejected a short-term ceasefire and that Putin’s terms for peace are tantamount to a full surrender. Meanwhile, another difficult winter looms for Ukrainian civilians, with a critical munitions shortage limiting Zelenskyy’s ability to defend infrastructure against Russian strikes. Zelenskyy said he was due to speak to U.S. negotiators by phone later Sunday and was still hopeful of a meeting in the days ahead. “I’m very open for this, even with all the difficult circumstances,” he said. He cited some progress after a multiday interruption to U.S. intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which he said has now been “deblocked.” “We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.” European and Ukrainian officials previously told NBC News they believed that a move to limit sharing intelligence , coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks. While Zelenskyy indicated that the intelligence problem has been resolved, he said that Ukraine was still facing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service. Asked if he thought Trump or Musk had directly made the decision to limit Starlink, Zelenskyy said that he didn’t know but thought “both” were involved. He said that if Trump decided tomorrow to lift the restriction, “it will immediately work as it was before.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. item.title: A new generation of synthetic drugs is changing America's overdose crisis
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raid Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says. The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars. "You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says. He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune. We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction. Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs. "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanyl [Darren Conway/BBC] Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets [Darren Conway/BBC] We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States. At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over. It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl. The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added. When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce." Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me. They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat. Recovery group offering hope At the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma. They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty. One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life. As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid. "It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement. Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood Church [Darren Conway/BBC] One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time [Darren Conway/BBC] Both in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose". "In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers. Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so. "The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it." Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope Dealers [Darren Conway/BBC] Overdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds. His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina. That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine. "The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements." And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois. Watch the documentary on YouTube I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity. Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means. He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever. When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability." And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear. "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me. A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening. "In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel." The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures. Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens. It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters. "Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained. Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures. In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in letters [Darren Conway/BBC] In August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search. As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of. As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates. The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper. Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected. Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moisture [Darren Conway/BBC] Outside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them. In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell. Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs. She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing." Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants. The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous". "Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me. Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town [Darren Conway/BBC] Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics. "The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it." Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way." 'A lot of people are struggling' Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track. It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb. Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs [Darren Conway/BBC] As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed." A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail. When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours." She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs." Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics. Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them. item.title: Jackson doesn't regret telling Collins to 'shut up' after protester interrupted debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should “shut up” after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign's backers. "She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth-term. He spoke in an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” that aired Sunday. During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race, as the Nov. 3 election nears a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group's page said: “We’re proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday.” The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Maine, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had “zero coordination” with Jackson's campaign. "I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all,” he was quoted as saying. The Sunrise Movement is a left-wing political advocacy organization that champions the Green New Deal, aimed at transitioning the U.S. economy to 100% renewable energy. The group, which has local arms around the country, regularly organizes protests, sit-ins and climate strikes. Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates. “But what I’m not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins,” he said. He added: "I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I’m not going to apologize for that.” Collins told Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Friday that she was “struck by how reflective the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was.” Collins said "the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.” She cited what she said was “the reputation” that Jackson had in the Legislature “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn’t surprise me.” Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, "I wear my heart on my sleeve.” He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time. Jackson was asked on CNN about some Republicans who are saying there were stories that he was aggressive in his tone to women from his time in the Legislature and that his remark Thursday night was another example of that. Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions “attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn’t surprise me." item.title: Carney says 4 service members killed, dozens injured in fire at Alberta military base
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
EDMONTON, Alberta (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta, describing it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil. Fire crews scrambled late Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications that the incident was the result of terrorism, but the cause remained under investigation. Speaking in a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving. Carney said the service members killed and injured were participating in military training when the fire broke out Saturday. Flags would fly at half-staff on federal buildings across the country in honor of those affected by the tragedy, he said. Carney said those affected included reservists and soldiers from Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, one of Canada’s most storied military regiments. The personnel had come from bases across the country to train at Wainwright. It was not immediately clear exactly how many people had been injured. Carney said the wounded were being treated in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary. Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among the military personnel critically injured. “As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta. A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (112 miles) northwest, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were taken to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care. “This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster.” Hospitals declare emergency Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a “Code Orange,” an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients require coordinated medical care. The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that extremely few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area. It urged people to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible. Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised the response of local medical personnel. He said helicopters and planes had been transporting patients to other facilities for treatment. At least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health center late Saturday as paramedics and soldiers rushed about. One patient was seen being loaded into an ambulance. The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents. Military rules out terrorism as cause Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as “very, very active and delicate.” He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information. Two people, including a 6-year-old boy, were killed and 11 others injured after a truck drove through a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday afternoon, police said, in what officials called a "heartbreaking" incident that authorities are still investigating. First responders rushed to Stryker Soccer Complex after receiving multiple 911 calls around 3:25 p.m. CT, Capt. Aaron Moses of the Wichita Police Department told reporters at a press conference Saturday evening. KAKE - PHOTO: In this image taken from a video, police respond to the scene at the Stryker Sports Complex. Police said the driver, who they identified only as a 34-year-old woman of Garden City, Kansas, stayed with the truck after the incident. "She has been cooperative to this point in the investigation," he said, adding later she was in police custody. Moses told reporters he believed one of the driver's children was playing soccer at the complex on Saturday but was not on that field at the time of the incident. KAKE - PHOTO: First responders are shown at the scene of an incident at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Oct. 17, 2026. There were two juveniles who were also inside the truck at the time it went onto the field, police said. When police arrived at the scene, the truck was located on the west end of the field and bystanders were helping to render aid to the injured people on the field, Moses said. The two people who died -- a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man, both of McPherson, Kansas -- were pronounced dead on the scene, police said. Of the 11 people who were injured and taken to the hospital, five are children, ranging in age from 5 to 9. Wichita Police Department - PHOTO: In this screen grab from a video posted to social media, Captain Aaron Moses of the Wichita Police Department speaks to the media on Oct. 17, 2026, in Wichita, Kansas. The injured adults range in age from 28 to 68. Of the injured, 10 had "traumatic injuries," Moses said, saying they ranged from bruises to "extremely severe injuries." Police stressed they are still investigating and asked the public for patience. "We know what happened, but now we're working very hard to find out why it happened, and we're not there yet," Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan told reporters. Police said they have interviewed over 30 witnesses at the scene and are asking anyone with pictures or video of the incident to share them with investigators. Police also credited bystanders who the police chief said "sprang into action so quickly and gave life-saving assistance until the arrival of first responders." Sullivan added, "It was truly amazing, but I think it's indicative of the of the Wichita community." Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said "Tonight, Wichita grieves together." "Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita," Mayor Lily Wu told reporters. "Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon watching their children play soccer. No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold." The city of Wichita said in a Facebook post Saturday afternoon that all events at the sports complex have been canceled until further notice. KAKE - PHOTO: First responders are shown at the scene of an incident at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Oct. 17, 2026. "We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time," the city said in a statement. Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly said in a statement she was monitoring the situation and in touch with the mayor. KAKE - PHOTO: First responders are shown at the scene of an incident at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Oct. 17, 2026. "My condolences go out to the families of the victims, the survivors, and all those impacted by this event," Kelly said in a statement. In a statement, the Stryker Soccer Complex said it was praying for those affected. "Our hearts are heavy as we process the tragic events at Stryker today," the statement said. "We are holding everyone impacted, the injured, their families, and all those who witnessed this heartbreaking event close in our thoughts and prayers." ABC News' Chris Barry, Brianna Sanchez and Michael Pappano contributed to this report. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
